question: How does a linear search find an item in a list?
correct: It checks each item in order until it finds a match or runs out of items
incorrect: It jumps to the middle and discards half the list each step
It sorts the list first and then reads off the last item
It looks the item up directly from its value, with no comparing
feedback: Linear search makes no assumptions about order, so it has no shortcut: it walks the list one item at a time. That is exactly why it works on an unsorted list.

question: A linear search over a list of 12 names looks for a name that is not in the list at all. How many comparisons does it make?
feedback: To be sure something is absent, the search has to rule out every item, so a miss always costs the full length. A lucky hit on the first item costs 1, and an average hit costs about half the list.

question: Why do these search functions return  None  rather than  -1  when the item is not found?
correct: -1 is a valid Python index, so a caller who skips the check gets the last item
incorrect: Python does not allow a function to return a negative number
None is faster for Python to return than a small integer
-1 would be confused with the item stored at position 1
feedback: In Python items[-1] is the last item, so returning -1 for 'not found' can hide a bug. There is no items[None], so a mistake fails loudly and immediately instead.

question: What must be true of a list before binary search will work on it?
correct: It must already be sorted
incorrect: It must contain only numbers, not text
It must have an odd number of items
It must be shorter than a few thousand items
feedback: Binary search decides which half to throw away by comparing with the middle item. That decision is only trustworthy if the list is in order — which is why sorting is worth the effort.

question: What does binary search do on each pass?
correct: Compares the middle item to the target and discards the half that cannot contain it
incorrect: Compares the first two items and swaps them if they are out of order
Removes the middle item and searches the rest from the start
Splits the list into single items and merges them back in order
feedback: This is how you look a word up in a dictionary: open to the middle, decide whether the word is earlier or later, and ignore the half it cannot be in. Each look halves what remains.

question: You run binary search on a list that turns out NOT to be sorted, and it reports that an item is missing even though the item is in the list. Why is this failure especially dangerous?
correct: It fails silently, giving a wrong answer instead of an error
incorrect: It permanently reorders the list while searching it
It keeps searching forever instead of stopping
It deletes the item it failed to find from the list
feedback: Binary search trusts the ordering, so on shuffled data it rules out the wrong half and confidently reports nothing found. An error you can see is far easier to fix than a wrong answer you cannot.

question: Match each Big-O growth rate to what it describes.

pairs.definition: The same work no matter how big the input is
Each step throws away a fraction of what is left
Work grows in step with the size of the input
Work grows with the square of the input size

feedback: Big-O names the shape of the growth, not an exact step count. Constants and small terms are dropped: nobody says 3n plus 7 steps, they say O(n).

question: Which Big-O describes linear search, and which describes binary search?
correct: Linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n)
incorrect: Linear search is O(log n); binary search is O(n)
Both are O(n), but binary search has a smaller constant
Linear search is O(1); binary search is O(n log n)
feedback: Doubling the list doubles linear search's worst case, but adds only one step to binary search. Among a billion items, linear search may check a billion and binary search checks about 30.

question: Why does Big-O deliberately ignore constants, so that 3n + 7 steps is simply called O(n)?
correct: The point is how the work grows with input size, not the exact count on one machine
incorrect: Constants are too difficult to measure accurately in practice
Every algorithm turns out to have the same constants anyway
Constants only matter for programs that use a lot of memory
feedback: Actual seconds depend on whose computer you use. Growth shape does not — and it is what decides whether an algorithm still works when the data gets ten times bigger.

question: How does selection sort work?
correct: Find the smallest remaining item, swap it into the next slot, and repeat
incorrect: Split the list in half repeatedly, then merge the sorted halves
Compare neighbouring pairs and swap them until no swaps remain
Insert each item into a second list at the right position
feedback: The outer loop walks the slot being filled and the inner loop scans the unsorted tail for the smallest item. After each pass, the sorted front of the list grows by one.

question: Given  ranks = [7, 2, 10, 4, 1], what does the list look like after the FIRST pass of selection sort?
feedback: The first pass finds the smallest item (1, at the end) and swaps it with whatever was in slot 0. The 7 that was displaced moves to where the 1 had been.

question: Why is selection sort O(n squared)?
correct: For each of the n slots it scans the remaining items, so the work multiplies
incorrect: It has to sort the list twice to be certain it is in order
Each swap requires copying the whole list into a new one
It compares every item to every other item exactly twice
feedback: A scan inside a loop means roughly n times n comparisons. Fine for a handful of cards; for a million items that is about a trillion comparisons.

question: Merge sort uses divide and conquer. Which description matches it?
correct: Split until each pile is one item, then merge sorted piles upward
incorrect: Scan for the smallest item, place it, and repeat on the rest
Sort the first half completely, then append the second half unsorted
Compare the first and last items and work inwards to the middle
feedback: A single item is already sorted, and merging two sorted piles is cheap. There are about log n levels of splitting, each doing O(n) merging work, which is where O(n log n) comes from.

question: Which of these are true about  sorted(items)  and  items.sort()? (Select all that apply)
correct: sorted(items) returns a new list and leaves the original alone
items.sort() rearranges the original list and returns None
incorrect: Both leave the original list unchanged
sorted(items) only works on lists of numbers
items.sort() must be given a key function to work
feedback: Writing x = mylist.sort() and getting None back is a classic beginner bug. Use sorted() when you want a new list, and .sort() when you mean to rearrange the original in place.

question: In  sorted(hand, key=lambda c: c.rank), what does the key function do?
correct: It is called on each item and returns the value to compare by
incorrect: It filters out the items that do not have a rank
It decides whether the result is ascending or descending
It gives the sorted list a name for later lookup
feedback: Python calls the key function on each card, gets back a rank number, and sorts by those numbers — without losing track of which whole card each number came from. In real code you rarely write a sort, but you constantly choose what to sort by.

question: You need to search a large collection many times, and you are free to prepare it first. Which approach is best?
correct: Sort it once, then use binary search for every lookup
incorrect: Use linear search each time and skip the sorting cost
Sort it again before every single lookup
Use selection sort during each lookup to find the item
feedback: Sorting is a one-time cost that makes every later search logarithmic. When you search a lot, that trade pays for itself quickly; for a single lookup on unsorted data, plain linear search is simpler.

question: A special return value meaning "not found", such as the None these search functions return, is called a ___ value.
correct: sentinel
feedback: A sentinel is a value chosen to signal a condition rather than to be real data. Choosing a safe one matters: -1 is a poor sentinel in Python because it is also a valid index.

question: In the worst case, how many comparisons does a linear search make on a list of {{n}} items?
feedback_template: Linear search may have to check every item, so the worst case is one comparison per item: {{expected}}. Double the list and you double the worst case.

question: A sorted list holds {{n}} items. In the worst case, how many times can binary search halve it before one item is left? (This is its worst-case number of comparisons.)
feedback_template: Each pass halves the range, so the count is how many times {{n}} can be halved: {{expected}}. That is the log-base-2 of the list size, which is what O(log n) means.

question: A selection sort runs on {{n}} items. Roughly how many comparisons does it make, using the rough n-times-n estimate for O(n squared)?
feedback_template: For each of the {{n}} slots it scans the rest of the list, so the work is on the order of {{n}} times {{n}} = {{expected}} comparisons.

question: What is a Turing machine?
correct: A thought experiment: an endless tape, a read-write head, and a small rulebook
incorrect: The first electronic computer, built at Bletchley Park in 1943
A machine that decides whether any given program will halt
A modern processor design that runs one instruction per cycle
feedback: Turing stripped computation down to the simplest possible device in order to reason about what computing is at all. It was never meant to be built and used.

question: What does the Church-Turing thesis claim?
correct: Anything that can be computed at all can be computed by a Turing machine
incorrect: Any program that halts can be made to run in reasonable time
Every problem has an algorithm if you look hard enough
Turing machines are faster than the computers we build today
feedback: This is why we can speak of computation as one universal idea rather than a different idea per machine. Your phone can compute no class of things that the tape-and-rulebook gadget could not.

question: What is the halting problem?
correct: Deciding, for any program and input, whether that program will eventually stop
incorrect: Deciding how many steps a program will take before it stops
Stopping a program safely once it has already started running
Finding the input that makes a program run for the longest time
feedback: Turing proved in 1936 that no program can answer this correctly for every case. The proof builds a program that asks the halting-detector about itself and then does the opposite of whatever it predicts.

question: What does it mean to say the halting problem is undecidable?
correct: No algorithm can answer correctly in every case, whatever its resources
incorrect: The problem takes so long to solve that nobody has finished yet
The answer depends on which programming language is used
The problem can be solved but only by a quantum computer
feedback: Undecidable is not the same as hard. A hard problem can be solved slowly; an undecidable one has no correct general algorithm at all — faster hardware changes nothing.

question: Real tools such as antivirus scanners and infinite-loop detectors exist even though the underlying questions are undecidable. How is that possible?
correct: They settle for being usually right, or right on a restricted set of cases
incorrect: They run the program to completion first and then report
They rely on hardware that is not a Turing machine
They only work on programs written without any loops
feedback: Undecidability rules out a perfect general answer, not a useful partial one. Practical tools trade completeness for usefulness — which is why an antivirus can miss things and a type checker rejects some safe programs.

question: Which pair of statements correctly describes the classes P and NP?
correct: P problems can be solved quickly; NP problems can have a proposed answer checked quickly
incorrect: P problems are possible; NP problems are impossible for any computer
P problems need sorted input; NP problems work on unsorted input
P problems run on one processor; NP problems need many processors
feedback: Assembling a thousand-piece jigsaw may be brutal, but glancing at a finished one to confirm it is right is quick. That gap between finding and checking is what P versus NP is about.

question: Why is the question "does P equal NP?" famous?
correct: Nobody has proved it either way, and a proof would carry a million-dollar prize
incorrect: It was proved false in 1936 and is now only of historical interest
It asks whether any computer can outperform a Turing machine
It determines how fast a sorting algorithm is allowed to be
feedback: Almost everyone believes finding is genuinely harder than checking, but belief is not proof. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, and much of modern encryption quietly depends on the answer being no.

question: A headline claims a powerful enough AI will eventually solve any problem. Which response is accurate?
correct: An AI runs on ordinary computers, so undecidable problems stay out of reach
incorrect: AI systems are not algorithms, so the theory of computation does not apply
An AI can solve undecidable problems if it is given enough training data
Undecidable problems become decidable once enough computers work together
feedback: The limit is mathematical, not a matter of scale or training. It is worth separating two things: impossible in principle, like a perfect halting detector, and merely unreliable in practice, like hallucinating a fact.

question: Which of these are limits about cost rather than about impossibility? (Select all that apply)
correct: Finding the provably best packing for a truck full of oddly shaped boxes
Scheduling five hundred classes with no conflicts, guaranteed optimally
incorrect: Writing one program that decides whether any given program halts
Writing one checker that decides whether any two programs always agree
feedback: The first two are NP-style problems: solutions exist and can be checked quickly, but finding a guaranteed-best one may take impractically long. The last two are undecidable — no correct general algorithm exists at all.

question: A problem that can be solved in principle, but needs an impractical amount of work to solve, is called ___.
correct: intractable
feedback: Intractable sits between easy and impossible: the algorithm exists, but running it on a real input would take longer than anyone can wait.

question: Match each technique to when you would reach for it.

pairs.definition: The data is unsorted or the list is tiny
The data is sorted and you search it often
Learning how sorting works, or a very small list
Real code, where a fast built-in sort is wanted

feedback: In practice you almost never hand-write a sort. Knowing how they work is what lets you judge which tool fits and what it will cost.

question: Write the Python expression that returns a new list holding the items of  nums  in ascending order, without changing nums.
correct: sorted(nums)
feedback: sorted(nums) hands back a new sorted list. nums.sort() would rearrange the original instead and return None.
